title: Why Jesus Chose an Unlikely Tax Collector
paragraphs:
Why Jesus Chose an Unlikely Tax Collector
The Man Everyone Hated—And the Disciple Jesus Wanted
The crowd never saw it coming.
When Jesus of Nazareth walked toward the tax booth that day, nobody expected a miracle.
Yet one of the most shocking transformations in Scripture was about to unfold before their eyes.
Because sitting behind that tax table was a man everyone despised.

The dust of Capernaum swirled through the streets as merchants carried goods to market and fishermen unloaded their catches from the Sea of Galilee. Somewhere in the middle of ordinary life sat a man named Matthew.
In Hebrew, his name was Mattityahu (מַתִּתְיָהוּ), meaning “Gift of Yahweh.”
But nobody viewed him as a gift.
Tax collectors worked for Rome. They collected money from their own people and often enriched themselves through corruption. They represented oppression. They were symbols of betrayal.
To many Jews, tax collectors ranked alongside notorious sinners.
Yet Jesus walked directly toward one.
Scripture records the moment with stunning simplicity:
“Jesus saw a man called Matthew sitting at the tax office, and He said to him, ‘Follow Me.’ So he arose and followed Him.” (Matthew 9:9)
The Greek text is even more striking.
One moment he was collecting money.
The next moment he was following the Messiah.
Because when Jesus calls someone, He sees what nobody else sees.
Everyone else saw a tax collector.
This is one of the most beautiful themes running through all of Scripture.
“Man looks on the outward appearance, but the LORD looks on the heart.” (1 Samuel 16:7)
The Hebrew word for heart here is “lev” (לֵב).
In biblical thought, the lev was not merely emotions.
It represented the center of a person's being.
And that should stop every reader in their tracks.
Because many of us secretly believe our worst moments define us.
We assume God sees us the way people do.
But Matthew's story shatters that lie.
Jesus is not intimidated by your history.
He is not shocked by your failures.
He is not surprised by your secrets.
The cross was not Plan B.
Redemption has always been His specialty.
The same Savior who walked toward Matthew still walks toward people everyone else has given up on.
Matthew did not merely follow Jesus privately.
Luke's account tells us he hosted a great banquet.
Tax collectors and sinners filled the room.
The Pharisees could not understand why a holy teacher would share a table with such people.
But Jesus answered them with words that continue to shake generations:
“It is not the healthy who need a physician, but those who are sick.” (Luke 5:31)
The Greek word for physician is “ἰατρός” (iatros).
Someone who comes to the wounded.
Jesus never denied the reality of sin.
But He also revealed His mission.
The Gospel is not God looking for perfect people.
The Gospel is God rescuing broken people.
That truth explains why Matthew became one of the greatest witnesses to Christ in history.
The very man considered spiritually disqualified became the author of the first Gospel account.
The Holy Spirit entrusted a former tax collector with recording the life, teachings, death, and resurrection of Jesus Christ.
Only God writes stories like that.
Only Jesus turns scandals into testimonies.
Only grace transforms enemies into disciples.
Only the Gospel turns outsiders into family.
Matthew's Gospel eventually reached countless generations, nations, languages, and cultures.
Millions have encountered Jesus because one hated tax collector responded to a simple invitation:
Perhaps that invitation is reaching you today.
Maybe you have spent years running from God.
Maybe you believe your past is too dark.
Maybe shame has become your identity.
Maybe you've convinced yourself that Jesus could never use someone like you.
Because his entire life became evidence that Christ specializes in rewriting stories.
The Gospel does not minimize sin.
It does not leave people unchanged.
It transforms them from the inside out.
That transformation remains available because Jesus Christ went to the cross, died for our sins, and rose again on the third day.
The One who called Matthew eventually stretched out His hands for the very people who mocked Him.
The Savior who welcomed sinners carried their punishment.
The Messiah who offered grace paid its cost Himself.
That is why no one is beyond hope.
Maybe that is why Matthew's story continues to resonate so deeply.
Because every believer is, in one way or another, an unlikely disciple.
Every Christian is living proof that salvation is a gift, not an achievement.
Every testimony ultimately points to the same reality:
We were not rescued because we deserved it.
We were rescued because Christ is merciful.
And if Jesus could transform a tax collector into a Gospel writer, imagine what He can do with a life fully surrendered to Him.
Someone in your circle may be carrying silent shame, believing their story is over when Jesus is just beginning to write a new chapter.
Your testimony may become the encouragement someone else desperately needs today.
Because somewhere right now, another Matthew is sitting at a table of regret, unaware that Jesus is already walking toward him.
